action_criteria.expected_evidence: Fibrillation and fasciculation potentials in the tongue, hand muscles, T7 paraspinals and right tibialis anterior, with chronic neurogenic change in the hand muscles; reduced median CMAPs with normal conduction velocities and no conduction block; normal sensory studies (limited by cooperation).
action_criteria.label: EMG and nerve conduction studies of the bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral regions to document lower motor neuron involvement and exclude conduction block and neuropathy
action_criteria.rationale: EMG/NCS confirms lower motor neuron involvement beyond the clinically affected muscles and excludes the main treatable mimics: multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block, demyelinating or sensorimotor neuropathy and myopathy. Gold Coast 2020 accepts EMG evidence of lower motor neuron dysfunction, and Awaji 2008 counts fasciculation potentials as active denervation in muscles with chronic neurogenic change.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: New bilateral motor cortex and corticospinal tract signal change since the MRI of 14 months ago (supportive only) and stable bifrontal and bitemporal atrophy; no restricted diffusion, infarct, haemorrhage or mass.
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI to exclude structural, vascular, demyelinating, inflammatory or neoplastic causes of the upper motor neuron or bulbar signs
action_criteria.rationale: MRI does not confirm ALS. It excludes brain and brainstem lesions that can cause upper motor neuron or bulbar signs, and here allows comparison with his MRI of 14 months ago for the frontotemporal atrophy; corticospinal tract signal change, when present, is supportive only.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal cervical and thoracic spine MRI: no cord compression or cord signal change.
action_criteria.label: Spine MRI of the cervical and thoracic cord, and of the lumbosacral spine when lower limb signs need it, to exclude compressive myelopathy, radiculopathy and other cord lesions
action_criteria.rationale: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy with radiculopathy is the commonest structural mimic of combined upper and lower motor neuron signs in the limbs. Spine MRI excludes it, but incidental spondylosis does not explain bulbar signs or denervation in other regions and must not delay the ALS work-up.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: CK 682 U/L (3.9x ULN); blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes, calcium, thyroid function, vitamin B12, folate, ESR and CRP normal.
action_criteria.label: Blood tests for treatable mimics and a pre-treatment baseline: full blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes and calcium, CK, thyroid function, vitamin B12 and folate, ESR and CRP
action_criteria.rationale: These tests exclude metabolic, endocrine, nutritional and inflammatory mimics and give the liver and blood-count baseline needed before riluzole; phenotype-specific tests are added only when the case raises that mimic.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: FVC 70% predicted and SNIP 48 cmH2O are reduced, without an AAN 2009 NIV marker yet.
action_criteria.label: Baseline respiratory function (FVC and SNIP, with MIP where available) to stage respiratory muscle involvement and plan monitoring and NIV
action_criteria.rationale: Respiratory function does not diagnose ALS. Once ALS is supported it stages respiratory muscle weakness, sets the baseline for 3-monthly monitoring and identifies patients who need early referral for NIV.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Pathogenic C9orf72 hexanucleotide repeat expansion; SOD1, TARDBP, FUS and TBK1 negative.
action_criteria.label: ALS gene panel (C9orf72 repeat expansion; SOD1, TARDBP, FUS and TBK1) after pre-test genetic counselling, once the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment is complete
action_criteria.rationale: Genetic testing does not make the diagnosis. It is offered with counselling to people with ALS because a pathogenic variant changes counselling for relatives and may open gene-targeted treatment or trials. His own frontotemporal dementia and his father's death at 62 from a nervous system disease that may have been FTD or ALS make a monogenic cause, most often a C9orf72 expansion, likely.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No clinically significant interaction with quetiapine, sertraline or amlodipine; oral suspension if tablets cannot be swallowed safely; liver test monitoring with a stop threshold of ALT above 5x ULN.
action_criteria.label: Check riluzole against the current medicines, alcohol use and liver function before the first dose, once the diagnosis is established
action_criteria.rationale: Riluzole is metabolised by CYP1A2 and can raise liver transaminases, so the medicine list, alcohol use and baseline liver function are reviewed before treatment. Quetiapine, sertraline and amlodipine do not interact with it; his choking episodes make the oral suspension the safer formulation if tablets cannot be swallowed.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not treat ALS with corticosteroids, IVIG or plasma exchange: they have no benefit.
Do not wait for FVC to fall below 50% or for respiratory symptoms before referring for NIV assessment.
Do not delay the swallowing assessment in a patient who is already choking or coughing on food or fluids.
Do not attribute the new weakness, wasting, dysarthria and choking to the frontotemporal dementia.
required_recommendations: Make and explain the diagnosis of ALS by Gold Coast 2020 criteria: progressive bulbar and limb weakness with upper motor neuron signs (brisk jaw jerk, limb hyperreflexia, bilateral Hoffman and Babinski signs, spastic gait) and lower motor neuron involvement in the bulbar and cervical regions on examination and EMG, with active denervation also in thoracic and lumbosacral muscles, with mimics excluded by MRI and blood tests, as part of one ALS-FTD spectrum with his frontotemporal dementia; disclose it in a planned face-to-face discussion with the patient and family.

Arrange a speech and language therapy swallowing assessment now (aspiration risk, safe food and fluid consistencies) and a dietetic review with baseline weight, and discuss gastrostomy early, while FVC is above 50% predicted; involve his wife in supervising meals while he has choking episodes.
Assess decision-making capacity for each major decision (riluzole, genetic testing, NIV, gastrostomy), involve his wife as caregiver, and plan advance decisions early while he can contribute.

Refer to the respiratory/NIV service now because FVC (70% predicted) and SNIP (48 cmH2O) are already reduced; screen for orthopnoea and nocturnal hypoventilation with overnight oximetry or capnography, and repeat FVC and SNIP within 3 months.

Offer riluzole 50 mg twice daily. Measure liver transaminases before the first dose, monthly for 3 months, every 3 months for the rest of the first year and periodically thereafter; stop riluzole if ALT exceeds 5x the upper limit of normal, and ask the patient to report any febrile illness so that neutropenia can be excluded.
Use riluzole oral suspension if tablets cannot be swallowed safely.

Refer to a specialist ALS multidisciplinary team (neurologist, specialist nurse, respiratory, speech and language therapy, dietetics, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and palliative care), reviewed about every 2 to 3 months, with an early, patient-paced discussion of advance care planning.

Provide post-test genetic counselling about the C9orf72 expansion with his wife present, and offer counselling to his first-degree relatives, including his adult son, each of whom has a 50% chance of carrying it, about the ALS and frontotemporal dementia risk, with predictive testing only after counselling.

avoided_actions.rationale: ALS is a motor-neuron disease without cortical electrical signature; EEG has no diagnostic role and adds cost without benefit.
Echocardiography is unrelated to ALS diagnosis; no indication absent comorbid cardiac disease.
Cardiac monitoring has no role in ALS diagnostic workup.
MRI is the standard structural study for ALS workup; head CT adds no diagnostic value and exposes the patient to ionizing radiation.
Amyloid PET has no role in ALS diagnosis (motor-neuron rather than amyloid pathology) and carries a high cost.
DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic integrity; it has no role in ALS, which spares the dopaminergic system.
FDG-PET has no established diagnostic role in ALS and adds substantial cost.

key_clinical_evidence: Gold Coast 2020: ALS needs progressive motor impairment with upper and lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least one body region, or lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least two, after other diseases are excluded. Here: brisk jaw jerk, limb hyperreflexia, bilateral Hoffman and Babinski signs and a spastic gait, with lower motor neuron involvement in the bulbar and cervical regions, with active denervation also in thoracic and lumbosacral muscles.
EMG lower motor neuron evidence is chronic neurogenic change with active denervation; by Awaji 2008 fasciculation potentials count as active denervation in a muscle with chronic neurogenic change.
Normal motor conduction velocities without conduction block argue against multifocal motor neuropathy, and normal sensory responses argue against a sensorimotor neuropathy or SBMA.
CK 682 U/L (3.9x ULN): mild to moderate elevation is common in ALS from denervation and does not by itself suggest a myopathy.

Reduced FVC (70% predicted) and SNIP (48 cmH2O) without an NIV marker yet. AAN 2009 markers that prompt NIV discussion are orthopnoea, FVC below 50% predicted, SNIP below 40 cmH2O, MIP weaker than -60 cmH2O or abnormal overnight oximetry; NIV prolongs survival and improves quality of life (Bourke 2006).
Bulbar involvement carries a worse prognosis and an aspiration risk; swallowing assessment and early gastrostomy discussion, while FVC is above 50% predicted, are priorities.

A C9orf72 repeat expansion is the commonest genetic cause of both ALS and FTD, so new motor neuron signs in bvFTD place him on the ALS-FTD spectrum, and each first-degree relative has a 50% chance of carrying it. Behavioural and executive impairment affects capacity, adherence and tolerance of NIV and gastrostomy, so decisions need capacity assessment and caregiver involvement.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The established bvFTD does not explain new tongue atrophy and fasciculations, limb wasting, upper motor neuron signs or multi-region denervation; these indicate motor neuron disease on the ALS-FTD spectrum, for which a C9orf72 expansion is the commonest shared genetic cause.

metadata.difficulty_rationale: Established bvFTD invites attribution of the new bulbar and limb signs to the dementia; the motor neuron disease must be recognised and the plan adapted to impaired capacity, choking and a familial C9orf72 expansion.
metadata.notes: ALS-FTD with a pathogenic C9orf72 expansion: new bulbar and limb upper and lower motor neuron signs with choking in a man with established bvFTD. The case turns on recognising the motor neuron disease rather than attributing it to the dementia, early swallowing and respiratory safety, capacity assessment with caregiver involvement, and genetic counselling for the family.

patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. M is a 67-year-old man with a diagnosis of behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) made 18 months ago based on personality change, disinhibition, executive dysfunction, and hypometabolism on FDG-PET in frontal and temporal regions. He has been managed with behavioral interventions and medications.

Over the past 6-7 months, his wife has noticed NEW motor symptoms: progressive bilateral arm weakness with visible muscle wasting of his hands, muscle twitching in his arms and calves, slurring of speech that is beyond his prior FTD-related dysexecutive speech pattern, and what appears to be tongue wasting. He has had difficulty with feeding himself and has had episodes of choking.

The new motor symptoms have emerged on a background of his established bvFTD and are being evaluated as a possible second, superimposed neurological process. His father died of a 'nervous system disease' at age 62.
